headline_marked: [[Crusoe abandons $1.25B plan]] to use Boom turbines at AI data centers
headline: Crusoe abandons $1.25B plan to use Boom turbines at AI data centers
summary: AI data center builder Crusoe has ended its agreement to purchase 29 42-megawatt Superpower turbines from Boom Supersonic, originally slated for 2027 deliveries.
details: Crusoe, a Denver-based AI data center startup, has officially terminated its $1.25 billion agreement with Boom Supersonic. The deal involved purchasing 29 of Boom's 42-megawatt Superpower turbines to power Crusoe's expanding AI data centers.

Boom Supersonic, primarily known for developing its Overture supersonic passenger jet, had launched a new business to sell stationary power plants. These Superpower turbines share about 80% of their parts with the jet's Symphony engine.

Boom CEO Blake Scholl announced the partnership's end on X, explaining that turbines are no longer part of Crusoe's near-term primary power mix. Crusoe confirmed the split, stating a need for flexibility in energy solutions as its portfolio evolves.

Crusoe's existing 1.2-gigawatt data center for Oracle and OpenAI in Abilene is powered by the grid, with a gas-turbine plant for backup. However, a new 900-megawatt data center for Microsoft in Abilene will utilize on-site gas turbines.

The cancellation represents a setback for Boom, which had raised $300 million last year largely to commercialize this new power plant venture. The company had planned to use profits from Superpower sales to fund the development of its Overture jet.

headline_marked: [[Tesla workers resist training Optimus robots]] designed to replace them, facing production hurdles
headline: Tesla workers resist training Optimus robots designed to replace them, facing production hurdles
summary: Tesla aims for 1,000 Optimus robots per week by late 2026, but is grappling with complex manufacturing, AI limitations, and employee pushback against training their future replacements.
details: Tesla's ambitious goal to produce 1,000 Optimus humanoid robots weekly by the end of 2026 is facing significant challenges. These include complex robot hands, manufacturing difficulties, and resistance from employees tasked with training their potential replacements.

CEO Elon Musk has called Optimus potentially "the biggest product ever," despite acknowledging that creating an autonomous, general-purpose humanoid robot is "one of the hardest things to solve." Extensive reporting by The Information has detailed multiple complications in development and mass production.

As of May 2026, Tesla's Fremont factory has reportedly ceased production of the Model S sedan and Model X SUV. The company has shifted both line workers and engineers to focus on the Optimus project, highlighting its strategic importance.

The newest iteration, Optimus V3, presents manufacturing hurdles, including difficulties with precise component alignment and limitations on production line speed. While production has scaled to hundreds per week, the target of over 1,000 weekly robots by late 2026 remains a stretch.

A major engineering challenge lies in creating robotic hands capable of delicate manipulation. Optimus's hands and forearms contain over 100 small components, requiring manual assembly by human workers, which adds to production complexity.

This manually intensive process has resulted in newly produced robots needing immediate fixes. Touch sensors for the hands have also been unreliable, leading Tesla to develop replaceable glove-like sensor layers instead of replacing entire robot hands.

Optimus's AI capabilities are reportedly still insufficient for general-purpose operations, a common hurdle for robotics companies. Sources indicate that current Optimus robots require specific programming for tasks in controlled environments.

To gather crucial training data for robots to learn tasks visually, Tesla initially had factory workers wear special suits to record movements. However, some workers complained, knowing the robots were designed to replace them, prompting Tesla to shift data collection to dedicated teams and "training hubs."

Tesla also relies on Chinese suppliers for various robot components, reflecting a broader US robotics industry dependence on China. This persists despite efforts to boost domestic supply chains and recent FCC bans on new foreign-made robots.

Many of Tesla's challenges in developing humanoid robots are not unique to the company. However, Tesla faces stiff competition from other automakers and robotics companies globally, making the successful scaling of Optimus a critical endeavor.
